title: Linux systemd Service Management
description: Learn to manage system services with systemctl and inspect logs with journalctl on modern Linux distributions.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, nginx.service is installed, unmasked, and stopped. You are an ordinary user with sudo access; system service changes require elevation. Use systemctl to start nginx immediately.
tasks.hint: Use systemctl start: 'sudo systemctl start nginx'
tasks.explanation: 'systemctl start' activates a unit (service) right away without changing its enabled/disabled state at boot.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, apache2.service is running and allows manual stopping. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use systemctl with elevation to stop this system service.
tasks.hint: Use systemctl stop: 'sudo systemctl stop apache2'
tasks.explanation: sudo systemctl stop asks the system manager to deactivate apache2.service. It uses the unit's configured stop behavior and may force termination after a timeout. It does not disable future boot activation.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, mysql.service is installed and running. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use systemctl with elevation to restart this system service (stop then start).
tasks.hint: Use systemctl restart: 'sudo systemctl restart mysql'
tasks.explanation: restart stops and starts mysql.service, unlike reload, which asks a running service to reread its own configuration. Restarting an inactive service would start it. sudo authorizes the system-manager change.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, docker.service is installed, unmasked, and has boot-install settings but is disabled. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use systemctl with elevation to enable it for boot without starting it now.
tasks.hint: Use systemctl enable: 'sudo systemctl enable docker'
tasks.explanation: enable creates links based on docker.service's [Install] settings so its boot target pulls it in. It does not start the service immediately; --now would also start it and is outside this request. sudo is needed to modify system unit links.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, ssh.service is installed. Your ordinary account may query system unit status and read its recent journal entries. Use systemctl to inspect this system service's detailed status.
tasks.explanation: systemctl status shows the unit's load and activation state, process information, and recent accessible journal entries. The .service suffix can be omitted. This account has read permission, so inspection needs no sudo.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, an administrator has changed system unit files under /etc/systemd/system. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use systemctl with elevation to make the system manager reread those files.
tasks.explanation: daemon-reload reruns generators, rereads unit files, and rebuilds systemd's dependency tree. It does not restart services or reload a service's own configuration. sudo supplies authorization for the system manager.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd-journald, your ordinary account has sudo access but no permission to read system logs directly. Use journalctl with elevation to follow the local journal in real time, including system entries, without a unit filter.
tasks.explanation: -f (or --follow) shows recent journal entries and then streams new ones. sudo grants access to system entries that this account cannot otherwise read. With no unit filter, output includes all accessible local journal sources.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, nginx.service has journal entries. Your ordinary account has sudo access but cannot read system logs directly. Use journalctl with elevation to show only nginx.service's journal entries since local midnight today.
tasks.hint: Combine elevation, unit filtering, and a start time: 'sudo journalctl -u nginx --since today'
tasks.explanation: -u (or --unit) selects nginx.service, including relevant manager messages about that unit. --since today starts at 00:00 in the host's local time; it is not the last 24 hours. sudo grants access to the required system logs.
